rich_summary: This section explains the myth behind Vishnu’s horse‑headed form (Hayasiras/Hayagriva) and the recovery of the Vedas. King Janamejaya asks why the Supreme Lord once appeared with an equine head. Vaisampayana responds by describing cosmic dissolution and creation: the elements merge successively until only the Supreme remains, from whom Brahma emerges upon the lotus. Two demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, born from drops within the lotus and embodying the qualities of Tamas and Rajas, steal the Vedas from Brahma and hide them in the cosmic waters. In despair, Brahma praises Narayana, who awakens from yogic sleep, assumes a radiant horse‑headed form embodying the cosmos, retrieves the Vedas, and later slays the demons. The passage emphasizes Narayana as the ultimate source, sustainer, and inner soul of all phenomena, presenting a theological vision in which all elements, philosophies, and cosmic processes culminate in him.

highlight_spans.why: Establishes Vyasa as a manifestation of Narayana and frames the discourse’s authority and sacred lineage.
Part of the extended praise of Narayana as the supreme refuge and cosmic foundation, a core theological theme of the passage.
Introduces the central narrative question about Vishnu’s mysterious horse‑headed manifestation witnessed by Brahma.
Brahma laments the theft of the Vedas, a dramatic moment that motivates divine intervention.
Describes the cosmic horse‑headed form of the Lord whose body contains elements of the universe, a vivid mythic image.

top_scenes.scene_text: The cosmic horse‑headed form of Vishnu appears, its body made of the universe—sun and moon as eyes, Ganga and Saraswati as limbs, and the starry sky as its crown.
Brahma sits upon the radiant lotus in the endless cosmic ocean, grieving as the demons Madhu and Kaitabha dive away with the stolen Vedas.
The two fierce Asuras confront Narayana reclining upon the serpent in the cosmic waters before their final battle.
